prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Heeeey reddit wtf is that and why isn't alcohol working?

This was my very first syngonium. I absolutely will. Not. Lose. It. It started my love for syngoniums and i just cannot lose it. I have sprayed this thing down so many times in the last few weeks. I've used peroxide, alcohol, insecticide, neem, I tried fungicide as a last ditch! What is is and how to I make them disappear!?

I've had a nasty mealy problem for the last year ish but haven't lost a plant yet. These didn't look like mealies to I wasn't too sure what to do and everything either reeks and isn't working or smells slightly better and still isn't working.

An automatic image classifier was also run on each photo. It only knows 5 classes:
- healthy: no visible problem
- watering: wilting or withering from too little or too much water
- fungal_bacterial: leaf spots, rust, anthracnose, blight, rot, bacterial wilt
- pest: visible insects or mites (trained almost only on cochineal scale on cactus)
- other: anything else, e.g. sunburn, nutrient or mineral problems, viruses, leaf tip necrosis, cold damage

The classifier is not perfect. It was trained mostly on curated dataset photos, not on phone photos like these,
and on such photos it is often wrong while still reporting a very high probability. Treat it as one weak hint:
rely on what you see in the photos and on the post first.

Classifier output (probability of each class):
Photo 1: watering 97%, fungal_bacterial 2%, other 1%, healthy 0%, pest 0%
Photo 2: healthy 51%, fungal_bacterial 25%, watering 23%, other 0%, pest 0%

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely cause: mealybugs.** The white, waxy, cottony specks where the leaves meet the stems and along the leaf surfaces are the classic mealybug signature, and the shiny, sticky coating on the stems is probably honeydew they leave behind. The browning and crisping leaves are likely damage from them feeding. Since you've dealt with mealies before, this may be a recurrence. The photos don't show webbing, so spider mites are less likely.

**Why the alcohol isn't working:** Mealybugs hide in leaf axils, along stem bases, and under the leaf sheaths, and their waxy coating shrugs off a spray. Light misting mostly misses them, and eggs survive a single treatment. Fungicide and peroxide won't touch pests at all.

**Fix:**

1. **Isolate the plant** away from your others, and check your other plants and the soil surface.
2. **Remove pests by hand.** Dip a cotton swab in 70% isopropyl alcohol and dab every visible mealybug and cottony mass, especially where the petioles meet the stems and under the leaf sheaths near the soil. Do this carefully so you don't rub off the stems.
3. **Remove badly damaged leaves** (the crispy brown ones) to reduce hiding spots. Cut them at the base with clean scissors.
4. **Repeat every 5–7 days for 3–4 weeks.** That covers at least two life cycles so you catch the hatchlings. If it keeps coming back, a systemic insecticide (imidacloprid-based, applied to the soil) is the most reliable option, following the label.

Also check the roots and the soil around the base for cottony masses before repotting, and only repot if the roots look healthy. Water only once the top inch of soil is dry, since the plant has crispy leaves and you want to rule out underwatering.
